author: Independent education critic subagent (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5); did not author these pages; reviewed artifact bytes, manifests, intake, sources list and prerequisite pages only

findings.claim: The Recap and Cheat sheet disclose all three answers before the learner commits. They sit outside the activity sections in section.pep-recap (line 604), are never hidden (only the activity sections get the hidden attribute in render(), and no CSS keys off data-pep-complete), so they render under Activity 1 from first load. The cheat sheet shows the exact Activity 1 fix ('<label for="email">', 'type="email" required', 'type="number" min="16" max="120" required', '<button>Join</button>'), the Activity 2 fix ('.card { box-sizing: border-box; }') and the Activity 3 trap ('5 == "5"; // true, converts'). The recap repeats them in prose ('a real <button> that submits the form', 'box-sizing: border-box keeps the whole box at the width you set', 'A spread copy is shallow'). On a review page, whose whole point is retrieval, a learner who scrolls once can read off every key.
findings.recommendation: Hide the recap and cheat sheet (both Recap section and .pep-cheat) until data-pep-complete is true, for example render them hidden and reveal them in renderProgress() when done === activities.length, while keeping them in print/no-JS output. Or rewrite the cheat sheet to general patterns that don't match these scenarios one-for-one (no Book Swap field names, no box-sizing: border-box on .card, no 5 == "5").

findings.claim: Activity 1 hint 2 gives the answer away by elimination. It says 'Each wrong option keeps one problem. Ask of each: does a placeholder stay the only name, does an ARIA role stand in for a native element, or do min and max sit on a field that ignores them?' That names exactly the one defect of options A, C and D, so the only option left is B. The contract (html-artifact-contract.md §Progressive optional hints) says a hint 'does not give the answer'.
findings.recommendation: Make hint 2 one more reasoning step without listing the distractors' defects. For example: 'Pick one field and one control. Ask what a screen reader announces once the field has text, and what Enter does when focus is on the Join control.' Let the per-option feedback name each defect after the commit.

findings.claim: Activity 3 teaches the exact traps right before the predict, which turns retrieval into recognition and contradicts the page's own 'Answer from memory first' (line 379) and the contract rule 'The learner predicts before any teaching.' The paragraph under the code says 'A spread copy makes a new outer array, but the objects inside are shared. reduce starts from the value you pass as its second argument ... == converts types before comparing, while === never does.' Those three sentences settle distractors B (no sharing), A (deep sharing incl. push) and C (== false). None of it is a new joining detail; it is the content being reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Move this 'Recall the pieces' paragraph into hint 1 or 2, or into the post-check feedback. Leave only the scenario sentence and the code above the options.

findings.claim: Array.prototype.join is used but never taught in the course. available.join(", ") decides the printed first line, and distractor A's 'Dune, Beloved' depends on knowing join's separator behaviour. A search of every html-and-css, javascript-fundamentals, dom-tooling-and-async and fetch-and-browser-client artifact.md finds no join() teaching; it only appears inside page scripts. The page doesn't teach it either, which breaks 'nothing used before it is taught'.
findings.recommendation: Either log the array directly, e.g. console.log(shelf.length, total, available) with options printed as [ 'Dune' ], which matches the console.log(a, b) form the arrays page uses, or add one short teaching clause before the code: 'join(", ") glues the items into one string with a comma and space between them.'

findings.claim: Objective o1 ('Choose the semantic regions, heading levels, labels, input types and native controls ...') isn't fully assessed. All four options are identical on 'header and main regions; h3 becomes h2', so the regions and heading-level parts are never discriminated: a learner who wouldn't fix the outline still scores correct. Only labels, input type and native button vary.
findings.recommendation: Either narrow o1 to labels, input types and native controls, or make one distractor vary the structure. For example, keep h3 or use section/div wrappers while everything else is right, and replace one existing distractor so that each option still differs by exactly one defect.

findings.claim: Activity 2 doesn't assess the width calculation in objective o2 ('Calculate a card's rendered width ...'). Only option C contains the fix box-sizing: border-box, so a learner who knows the fix (and the visible cheat sheet shows it) picks C without doing the arithmetic. The two 396 px options differ only in the fix, and the two wrong widths each come with a wrong fix.
findings.recommendation: Decouple the two parts so each matters. For example, use options '396 px + border-box' (correct), '390 px + border-box' (forgot border), '396 px + max-width query' and '358 px + overflow-x: hidden'. Or ask the width as a separate predict before the fix choice.

findings.claim: The feedback for Activity 2 option B misdiagnoses the misconception. 374 px = 358 + 16, which is padding counted on one side only and no border. But the feedback says 'The border counts too ... Without the border it would still be 390 px', which answers a learner who chose 390 (padding on both sides, border forgotten). A learner who picked 374 isn't told their actual error: padding and border apply on both sides. The box-model topic page uses this same 'adds ... once instead of on both sides' distractor.
findings.recommendation: Either change B's width to 390 px to match its current feedback, or rewrite B's feedback: '374 px counts the padding on one side only. Padding and border apply on both left and right: 358 + 16 + 16 + 3 + 3 = 396 px. Removing the border would still leave 390 px, wider than the 358 px column.'

findings.claim: The 'Where this fits' section sits before the Activity 1 task and points at the answer. Its Good fit says 'Page regions, heading outlines, labels, input rules and buttons that native elements already provide: they give names, keyboard support ...', which favours real labels over placeholders (rules out A) and a native button over an ARIA role (rules out C). The contract says the fit section 'contains no activity answer.' Together with the teaching note at line 393 ('A div with a click handler never submits anything, so those checks never run'), which on its own disqualifies any option that keeps the div, Activity 1 becomes mostly recognition.
findings.recommendation: Keep the decision (browser vs server responsibility; it's authentic), but rewrite the good fit at the level of the decision and not the fix list. For example: 'Constraints the user can fix immediately and that native HTML can express, so they get feedback before a round trip.' Consider moving the 'button submits; div does not' note into hint 1 or the feedback, since accessibility-basics already teaches that a role adds no behaviour.

findings.claim: The scenarios are partly re-skins of the prerequisite pages' own activities, not new cumulative problems. Activity 3's core (const b = [...a]; b[0].n = 2; b.push(...); console.log(a.length, a[0].n)) is the destructuring-and-spread page's trace with names changed. Activity 2's arithmetic repeats the box-model prediction (content-box adds padding and border on both sides). Activity 1's distractors are the forms page's 'type=text with min/max' and the accessibility page's 'role=button + tabindex'. A learner who remembers those pages recognises the answers, not the principles. The module brief asks for 'additional scenarios that mix topics'.
findings.recommendation: In each activity, add at least one twist that needs two topics together and that no topic page showed. For example: a nested object one level deeper with structuredClone vs spread, a three-column breakpoint where gap and border-box together decide the overflow, or a fieldset/legend grouping that the forms and accessibility pages taught separately.

findings.claim: The Markdown companion doesn't mirror the HTML structure. Under '## Cheat sheet' it dumps every hint as unlabelled 'Where to act / Next step' pairs: hint-1 summaries are dropped, hint-2 summaries come out as 'Another hint Another hint, 2 of 2 for Activity 1', and the sources list sits after the cheat-sheet code with no heading. The 'Where this fits', 'Your task' and 'What success looks like' content is missing. The contract says 'Headings and objectives match the HTML exactly'. The same pattern shows up in 136 of 245 artifact.md files, so this is likely a generator issue, not this page's.
findings.recommendation: Raise this with tooling: render hints under per-activity 'Hint 1 of 2 for Activity N' labels inside each activity, add a Sources heading, and include the fit and task blocks. No page-level change is needed if the generator is fixed.
